concepts.title: Writing Dockerfiles: Instructions and Layer-Cache Efficiency
concepts.description: Docker builds an image by executing Dockerfile instructions in order, caching the result of each one as a layer; ordering instructions from least-to-most frequently changing turns routine rebuilds from minutes into seconds, while getting the order backwards defeats the cache on every build.
learningObjectives: Write a basic Dockerfile using FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE, and CMD correctly and in a sensible order.
Explain how Docker decides whether to reuse a cached layer or re-run an instruction, including the extra rule for COPY/ADD.
Explain why one cache miss invalidates every layer below it in the Dockerfile, regardless of whether those later instructions themselves changed.
Reorder a Dockerfile so that installing dependencies is cached separately from copying application source code.
Explain the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT, and describe a case for combining them.
Explain what .dockerignore is for and how an unfiltered build context can defeat caching in surprising ways.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Basic Dockerfile
sections.body:
A Dockerfile reads top to bottom as a build script, and a handful of instructions cover most real-world use: FROM picks the base image everything else builds on, and must be the first instruction (only ARG may precede it); WORKDIR sets the working directory for every instruction after it, creating the directory if it doesn't exist, which is generally cleaner than littering cd calls inside RUN; COPY brings files from the build context (the directory you pointed docker build at) into the image; RUN executes a command inside the image during the build and commits its filesystem effects as a new layer; ENV sets an environment variable that persists both during the rest of the build and inside any container started from the resulting image; EXPOSE is documentation: it declares which port(s) the application listens on, but doesn't publish anything to the host, which is a separate step at docker run time covered in a later concept; and CMD sets the default command that runs when a container starts, covered below alongside ENTRYPOINT.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
ENV PORT=8000
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

Every instruction that touches the filesystem (RUN, COPY, ADD) produces its own layer, per the previous module. ENV, EXPOSE, and CMD only update image metadata; they show up in docker history as zero-size steps. WORKDIR adds a layer only when it has to create the directory.

sections.heading: The Build Cache: A Linear Chain, Not a Set
sections.body:
Docker's build cache works instruction by instruction, in file order, and is best understood as a chain rather than a bag of independent decisions. For each instruction, Docker checks whether a cached layer already exists that was built from the identical instruction text and the identical parent layer (the result of everything above it). If both match, Docker reuses the layer and runs nothing. If either doesn't match, that's a cache miss, and every instruction from that point down is also a miss, even if its own text hasn't changed, because its parent layer is now different. Cache validity cascades downward from the first miss; nothing below a miss can be a hit, however unrelated it looks.

COPY and ADD get one extra rule on top of the instruction-text comparison: Docker also computes a checksum of the files being copied and treats a change in that checksum as a cache miss, even if the COPY line's text is identical to last time. That makes sense (COPY exists to bring in file content, so a cache that ignored content changes would be wrong), and it's the mechanism the next section's ordering advice hinges on.

sections.heading: Ordering for Cache Efficiency: Put What Changes Least First
sections.body:
Combine the two facts from the previous section -- a miss cascades to everything below it, and COPY's cache validity depends on file content -- and a very common anti-pattern falls out:

```dockerfile
# Anti-pattern: source code changes invalidate the dependency install every time
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Here, COPY . . brings in the entire project, including application source files that change on nearly every commit. Because that COPY's checksum changes whenever any file in the project changes, even a one-character edit to a file npm install doesn't care about, the RUN npm install layer after it is invalidated on almost every build, forcing a full dependency reinstall even when package.json hasn't changed. For a project with a slow install step, that turns a near-instant rebuild into a multi-minute one on every commit.

The fix is to copy only the files that determine the install step's output before running the install, and copy the rest of the frequently-changing source afterward:

```dockerfile
# Cache-friendly: dependency install only reruns when package files actually change
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Now RUN npm ci's cache validity depends only on the checksum of package.json and package-lock.json, which change far less often than the rest of the source tree. A commit that only touches application code, and not the dependency manifests, hits the cache for the whole install step and only re-executes the final COPY . . (cheap, since it's just a filesystem copy) and whatever follows. The principle extends past this example: order instructions from least to most frequently changing, so that cache misses are confined to the smallest, cheapest suffix of the file on a typical day-to-day change.

sections.heading: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT, and the Exec-Form Signal-Handling Gotcha
sections.body:
CMD sets the default command for the container, but it's only a default: anything supplied after the image name in docker run image_name <this part> replaces it. ENTRYPOINT sets the command that always runs (unless you pass --entrypoint), and arguments given at docker run time are appended to it rather than replacing it. Combining them gives you a common, useful pattern: a fixed executable via ENTRYPOINT plus overridable default arguments via CMD:

```dockerfile
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]
CMD ["--port=8000"]
```

docker run myimage runs python app.py --port=8000; docker run myimage --port=9000 runs python app.py --port=9000. The entrypoint executable stays fixed, but the default arguments after it are swapped out. Contrast that with a CMD-only image, where supplying anything at docker run time replaces the entire command, executable included.

Separately, both instructions come in two forms, and the difference matters more than it looks. Exec form, CMD ["node", "server.js"], runs the given program directly as the container's PID 1. Shell form, CMD node server.js, runs /bin/sh -c "node server.js", so the shell, not your program, becomes PID 1, with node as its child. This matters because docker stop sends SIGTERM to PID 1 and waits a grace period (10 seconds by default) before escalating to SIGKILL. In shell form, that SIGTERM goes to the shell, which typically does not forward signals to its child (some shells exec a lone command, but you can't count on it). Your application never receives the shutdown signal, and docker stop waits out the full grace period and then kills the process with SIGKILL, skipping any graceful-shutdown logic, like closing DB connections or finishing in-flight requests. With exec form your program is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly (as PID 1 it only reacts if it installs a SIGTERM handler, since the kernel applies no default signal action to PID 1; docker run --init adds a small init process that covers this). Prefer exec form for both CMD and ENTRYPOINT unless you have a specific reason to need shell features like variable expansion or piping in the command line itself.

sections.heading: .dockerignore: Keeping Irrelevant Files Out of the Build Context
sections.body:
Before Docker evaluates a single instruction, it first sends the entire build context -- everything in the directory you pointed docker build at -- to the Docker daemon, and any COPY . . reads from that context. If that directory contains a bulky .git history, a node_modules folder installed on the host, log files, or editor scratch files, all of that is included in the context, slowing the initial context-transfer step of every build and, worse, factoring into COPY's content checksum. An unrelated change, like a new commit landing in .git's internal objects or a stray local log file being appended to, can then invalidate a COPY . . layer's cache though your application code hasn't changed.

```
# .dockerignore
.git
node_modules
*.log
.env
dist/
__pycache__/
```

A .dockerignore file, using the same pattern syntax as .gitignore, excludes matching paths from the build context entirely -- they're never sent to the daemon and never considered by any COPY instruction's checksum. Beyond caching, it's a security backstop: without it, a careless COPY . . can bake a local .env file full of secrets, or a whole .git history with old credentials in it, into an image layer. That's hard to undo, since removing the file in a later layer (see the multi-stage concept next) doesn't erase it from the earlier layer where it still sits.

examples.title: Cache-Busting vs Cache-Friendly Ordering, Side by Side
examples.code:
# BEFORE -- every source change forces a full reinstall
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# AFTER -- reinstall only happens when the dependency manifest itself changes
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
examples.explanation: In BEFORE, changing one line in server.js changes the checksum of COPY . ., which invalidates that layer's cache and, by the cascading rule, RUN npm install right after it, forcing a full dependency reinstall on nearly every rebuild whether or not any dependency changed. In AFTER, the first COPY depends only on package.json and package-lock.json, so RUN npm ci's cache validity is decoupled from application source changes: a typical commit that only touches server.js hits the cache for the often-slow install step and re-executes only the final, cheap COPY . . and anything after it. The two Dockerfiles produce functionally identical final images; only their rebuild speed on routine changes differs, often by minutes.

examples.title: Shell Form vs Exec Form: Who Receives SIGTERM
examples.code:
# Shell form -- /bin/sh becomes PID 1, node is its child
CMD node server.js

# Exec form -- node itself becomes PID 1
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
examples.explanation: CMD node server.js is shorthand Docker expands to CMD ["/bin/sh", "-c", "node server.js"], so the shell becomes the container's PID 1, with node running under it as a regular child. docker stop signals PID 1; in the shell-form container that's the shell, which typically doesn't forward signals to children, so node never sees the SIGTERM and docker stop waits the full grace period before killing everything with SIGKILL. CMD ["node", "server.js"] (exec form) skips the shell: node itself is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly. It still needs a SIGTERM handler, because PID 1 ignores signals it hasn't installed a handler for, but with one it can finish in-flight requests or close database connections before exiting, and docker stop returns quickly.

examples.title: ENTRYPOINT + CMD: A Fixed Binary With Overridable Default Args
examples.code:
FROM python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "manage.py"]
CMD ["runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
examples.explanation: ENTRYPOINT fixes python manage.py as the command that always executes; you can't accidentally run something unrelated to manage.py from this image without overriding it with --entrypoint. CMD's ["runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"] supplies default arguments appended after the entrypoint, and replaced wholesale, not merged, by whatever follows the image name in docker run. So docker run myimage runs python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 by default, while docker run myimage migrate runs python manage.py migrate. One image serves as both 'run the dev server' and 'run any other manage.py subcommand' just by changing the trailing arguments, with no second Dockerfile.

misconceptions.description: The Docker build cache looks at whether the Dockerfile as a whole has changed -- if it has, everything reruns; if it hasn't, nothing reruns.
misconceptions.clarification: The cache operates per instruction, in file order, not on the file as a single unit. Each instruction is checked independently against its own cached layer, matching instruction text plus, for COPY/ADD, matching file content checksums, and its specific parent layer. Editing line 8 of a 10-line Dockerfile reuses the cache for lines 1 through 7 exactly as before, and only lines 8 through 10 are re-executed -- it does not force a full rebuild from FROM, and conversely, an unchanged instruction can still be forced to rerun if something above it in the file changed, since its parent layer is now different.
misconceptions.fact: The cache operates per instruction, in file order, not on the file as a single unit.

misconceptions.description: Putting COPY . . right after FROM, before installing dependencies, is a harmless simplification -- it just means the files are available a bit earlier in the build.
misconceptions.clarification: It's not harmless: it typically defeats caching for every instruction after it. Because almost every commit touches something under the project root, an early COPY . . gets a new content checksum on nearly every build, which invalidates that layer and, by the cascading-miss rule, every instruction below it, including expensive steps like apt-get install, npm install, pip install, or a compilation step, forcing them to rerun in full on nearly every rebuild rather than only when their inputs changed.

exercises.prompt: Given this Dockerfile, a developer changes only a single line inside app.py, not requirements.txt, and reruns docker build. Which instructions get a cache hit, and which get re-executed?
exercises.code:
FROM python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
hints: COPY . . brings in the ENTIRE project directory -- does its checksum depend only on requirements.txt, or on every file underneath it?
If COPY . . gets a cache miss because app.py changed, what happens to every instruction listed after it in the file?
Compare this to the AFTER ordering from the explanation, where only files that actually affect the install step come before RUN pip install.
exercises.expectedAnswer: FROM and WORKDIR still hit the cache, since nothing about their inputs changed. COPY . . is a cache miss, because app.py, one of the files it copies, changed, which changes its overall content checksum. RUN pip install ... is ALSO forced to re-execute, only because it comes after the now-invalidated COPY, even though requirements.txt never changed and the list of dependencies is identical to last time.
exercises.solutionExplanation: COPY . . computes its cache validity from a checksum over every file it copies, which includes app.py, so changing one line in app.py changes that checksum and forces a cache miss on this COPY, even though requirements.txt is identical to the previous build. Because a miss cascades to every instruction below it, RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt is also forced to re-execute, reinstalling the same dependencies for no behavioral difference. This is the anti-pattern the ordering section warns about: copying requirements.txt separately, before the rest of the source, and running pip install against that narrower COPY would have let this build skip the reinstall.

exercises.prompt: A team's Docker image build takes 4 minutes on every single commit, even for one-line frontend tweaks, because npm ci reruns the full dependency install every time. Find the ordering problem in this Dockerfile and fix it.
exercises.code:
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
hints: COPY . . brings in the entire project before npm ci runs -- what specifically does npm ci's cache validity end up depending on, given that ordering?
npm ci only actually needs package.json and package-lock.json to determine what to install -- does it need the rest of the source tree at that point at all?
Split the single COPY . . into two COPY steps: one narrow one for just the files the install step needs, before RUN npm ci, and a second, broader one for everything else, after it.
exercises.solutionCode:
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original COPY . . before RUN npm ci ties the install step's cache validity to a checksum over the entire project, including every frontend source file, so any commit, even one that never touches package.json or package-lock.json, invalidates that COPY and forces a full npm ci rerun. The fix splits the COPY in two: a narrow one copying only package.json and package-lock.json before npm ci, so its cache validity depends only on the dependency manifests, and a broader COPY . . afterward for the rest of the source, which npm run build needs but which no longer affects npm ci's caching. A one-line frontend tweak now invalidates only the second COPY and what follows; the 4-minute install is a cache hit unless the manifests changed.

assessments.prompt: In a Dockerfile with five instructions in order, instruction #3 gets a cache miss because its instruction text, or, for COPY/ADD, its copied file content, changed since the last build. What happens to instructions #4 and #5, assuming their own text is completely unchanged from the last build?
options: Docker skips them entirely and reuses whatever the final image looked like last time.
They still get cache hits, since their own instruction text didn't change.
They are also forced to re-execute, because their cached layer's parent, the output of instruction #3, is no longer the same as it was last time.
Only #4 reruns; #5 can still be a cache hit as long as it doesn't reference anything from #3.
assessments.explanation: Cache validity for each instruction depends on both its own instruction, plus, for COPY/ADD, its file-content checksum, AND its specific parent layer being identical to last time. Once #3 misses, its own resulting layer differs from before, which makes it a different parent for #4 -- so #4 misses too, regardless of its own text, and the same logic cascades to #5. The “They still get cache hits, since their…” option is wrong because it ignores the parent-layer half of the cache check. The “Docker skips them entirely and reuses whatever…” option is nonsensical -- a miss doesn't cause Docker to silently reuse an old final result; it re-executes the remaining instructions. The “Only #4 reruns; #5 can still…” option is wrong because there's no per-instruction opt-out from the cascade based on whether an instruction references the earlier one -- the cascade is structural, based on layer parentage, not on any analysis of what each RUN command actually touches.

assessments.prompt: Besides comparing instruction text, what additional check does Docker perform specifically for COPY and ADD instructions when deciding whether to reuse a cached layer?
options: It always re-executes COPY and ADD on every build, since file operations can never be safely cached.
It computes a checksum over the actual content of the files being copied.
It checks whether the instruction appears at the same line number in the file as it did last time.
It checks only the copied files' last-modified timestamps on the host, ignoring their actual content.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer is the extra rule for COPY/ADD: cache validity depends on a checksum of the copied file content, not merely the instruction's text, since a content-blind cache would incorrectly ignore changes to the files being brought in. The “It checks whether the instruction appears…” option is wrong -- line position isn't part of the cache key at all. The “It checks only the copied files' last-modified…” option is wrong -- timestamps aren't what's compared; content checksums are, so an edit that changes a file's content is what matters. The “It always re-executes COPY and ADD…” option is wrong -- COPY/ADD absolutely can hit the cache, precisely when their content checksum and parent layer both match.

assessments.prompt: A Dockerfile uses `CMD node server.js` (shell form) instead of `CMD ["node", "server.js"]` (exec form). What concrete problem does this create when `docker stop` is run against a running container?
options: /bin/sh, not node, becomes PID 1, and since most shells don't forward SIGTERM to child processes by default, node never receives the signal.
docker stop fails outright with a permissions error and cannot stop the container.
node receives SIGTERM immediately regardless of form, since Docker signals every process inside the container simultaneously, not just PID 1.
Shell form causes the container to ignore docker stop entirely, requiring docker rm -f to remove it.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer describes the shell-form gotcha: CMD node server.js is expanded to /bin/sh -c "node server.js", making the shell PID 1 while node runs as its child, and since docker stop signals PID 1 and shells don't forward SIGTERM to children by default, node never sees the shutdown signal, forcing Docker to wait out the grace period and then SIGKILL everything. The “docker stop fails outright with a permissions…” option is wrong -- there's no permissions issue involved. The “node receives SIGTERM immediately regardless of form…” option is wrong: Docker signals PID 1 only, not every process in the container, which is the mechanism causing this bug. The “Shell form causes the container to ignore…” option is wrong -- docker stop still eventually succeeds via SIGKILL after the grace period; it doesn't require a forced removal.

assessments.prompt: A project's build context contains a large .git directory and a frequently-appended debug.log file, and no .dockerignore file exists. Beyond slower context transfer, what specific caching problem can this cause for a `COPY . .` instruction?
options: Docker automatically excludes .git and any *.log files from the build context even without a .dockerignore, so this scenario can't actually happen.
None -- .dockerignore only affects build speed, never caching correctness.
The build fails outright with an explicit checksum-mismatch error whenever .git or a log file is present in the context.

An unrelated change inside .git's internal objects, or a new line appended to debug.log, can change COPY . .'s overall content checksum, invalidating that layer's cache (and everything below it) for reasons that have nothing to do with actual application code changing.
assessments.explanation: Because COPY . . computes its cache validity from a checksum over everything in the context it copies, any file in that context changing, including incidental churn like .git's internal objects or an appended log line, changes that checksum and forces an unnecessary cache miss, cascading to every instruction below it. The “None -- .dockerignore only affects build speed…” option understates the effect -- .dockerignore is also a caching-correctness tool, not just a speed optimization. The “Docker automatically excludes .git and any *.log…” option is false -- Docker does not apply any exclusions on its own; only an explicit .dockerignore file does that. The “The build fails outright with an explicit…” option is false -- there's no explicit error; the build succeeds while re-executing more than it needs to.

assessments.prompt: Explain, using the mental model of a cache chain where a parent layer must match for a child layer to be reused, why moving COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ and RUN npm ci before COPY . . makes routine rebuilds of a typical Node.js project dramatically faster.
assessments.modelAnswer: Docker's build cache checks each instruction against two things: whether the instruction itself, plus, for COPY/ADD, a checksum of the files it copies, matches what produced the cached layer last time, and whether that cached layer's parent, the layer produced by the instruction directly above it, is also still the same. A miss at any point forces every instruction after it to be treated as a miss too, since their parent layer has now changed, even if their own text is unchanged. In a Dockerfile that does COPY . . before installing dependencies, that COPY's checksum depends on the entire project tree, which changes on nearly every commit, so it misses almost every build and drags RUN npm ci down with it, whether or not package.json changed. Reordering to COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ followed by RUN npm ci, with the full COPY . . after the install step, decouples the install step's cache validity from the rest of the source tree: it depends only on two files that change rarely compared to application code. When a commit only touches source files, that first COPY and the npm ci layer both hit the cache, and only the second, broader COPY and anything after it (like a build step) reruns, turning a multi-minute reinstall into a near-instant cache hit on most day-to-day builds.

assessments.prompt: Every CI build of your Node service takes 9 minutes because npm install runs from scratch each time, even when only one source file changed. Explain why and how you would restructure the Dockerfile.
assessments.modelAnswer: Docker caches each instruction as a layer and reuses it only if that instruction and everything before it are unchanged. If the Dockerfile does COPY . . before RUN npm ci, any source edit changes the copied files, invalidating the cache for the install step, so dependencies reinstall every time. Restructure so stable things come first: start from a pinned base image, COPY package.json and package-lock.json alone, RUN npm ci, and only then COPY the rest of the source and build. Add a .dockerignore excluding node_modules, .git and build output so the context is small and irrelevant changes do not bust the cache. In CI, persist the cache between runs (BuildKit cache mounts or registry cache with --cache-from), and consider a multi-stage build so the final image only contains production dependencies.

concepts.title: Multi-Stage Builds: Separating Build-Time From Run-Time
concepts.description: A multi-stage Dockerfile uses more than one FROM instruction to split the toolchain needed to build an application from the minimal runtime needed to run it, so the final image ships only what production actually needs, not the compilers, package caches, and source trees used to produce it.
learningObjectives: Explain the problem multi-stage builds solve: build tools and intermediate artifacts baked permanently into a production image.
Write a Dockerfile with multiple named FROM stages and use COPY --from=<stage> to bring specific artifacts forward.
Explain that each FROM starts a completely independent stage that does not automatically inherit any files from earlier stages.
Explain why a smaller final image matters beyond raw disk space, including attack surface and pull/deploy time.
Use docker build --target to build only up to an intermediate stage, and explain why naming stages is required for that to work reliably.

sections.heading: The Problem: Build Tools Don't Belong in the Thing You Ship
sections.body:
Building an application from source and running it are often two different jobs with different tool requirements. Compiling a Go binary needs the full Go toolchain; building a TypeScript frontend needs Node, npm, and every devDependency (bundlers, type checkers, test runners) that production has no use for; compiling a native C extension needs a C compiler and headers that the compiled shared library doesn't need at runtime. A single-stage Dockerfile that compiles and then keeps going, with CMD at the bottom of the same stage, bakes the whole build-time toolchain into the final image whether or not the running application ever touches it.

This has costs beyond untidiness: the image is much larger than it needs to be, so slower to pull and push and heavier on every node running it, and every package in that toolchain (a compiler, a package manager, dozens of transitive build dependencies) is one more thing a vulnerability scanner can flag a CVE against, though production never executes any of that code. Once the build is done, the toolchain is dead weight and attack surface.

sections.heading: Multiple FROM Instructions: Independent Stages, Explicitly Bridged
sections.body:
A multi-stage Dockerfile uses FROM more than once, optionally naming each occurrence with AS <name>:

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server .

FROM alpine:3.19
COPY --from=builder /out/server /usr/local/bin/server
ENTRYPOINT ["server"]
```

Each FROM starts an independent build stage, fresh from whatever base image it names; it does not inherit files, installed packages, or layers from any earlier stage. The builder stage above has the full Go toolchain and the source tree, but none of that exists in the second, unnamed, final stage unless it's explicitly brought over. COPY --from=builder /out/server /usr/local/bin/server is that explicit bridge: it reaches back into the builder stage's filesystem (that stage is never pushed or run as a container) and copies just the compiled binary into the final stage's own layers. Everything else in the builder stage, the Go compiler, the module cache, the .go sources, never makes it into the final image because nothing asked for it.

sections.heading: Sizing It Up: Before and After
sections.body:
Consider the same Go application built two ways. A single-stage build FROM golang:1.22, compiling in place and running from that same stage, ships an image that includes the entire Go toolchain (the golang:1.22 image is roughly 800MB) even though the running server needs none of it once the binary exists. A multi-stage build that compiles in a builder stage and copies only the resulting static binary into a minimal final stage, alpine, or even FROM scratch for a fully static binary with no OS at all, typically produces a final image in the 10-20MB range: the binary plus, at most, a thin base layer for basic OS utilities and CA certificates.

The application's behavior is identical either way; multi-stage builds are a packaging optimization, not a change to what the code does. What changes is the image as an artifact: it pulls in a fraction of the time, takes a fraction of the disk and registry storage, and presents a much smaller surface for a vulnerability scanner, since no compiler, package manager, or build-time dependency tree is left inside it. On platforms that scale out by frequently pulling fresh container instances, the smaller pull can also affect cold-start latency at the margins.

sections.heading: Intermediate Stages Also Cache, and --target Lets You Stop Early
sections.body:
Multi-stage builds aren't only about the final image: each stage caches independently, using the same per-instruction rules from the previous concept, which opens up a useful CI pattern. Consider splitting dependency installation, testing, and the final production build into their own explicitly named stages:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM deps AS test
COPY . .
RUN npm test

FROM deps AS build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:1.25-alpine AS production
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
```

docker build --target test -t myapp:test . builds only as far as the test stage. That's useful in CI, where you can run the test suite in the same environment the real build uses without producing, tagging, or storing the production image. docker build . with no --target builds the last stage, production here, and the stages it depends on. With BuildKit, the default builder in current Docker, the test stage is skipped in that build because production doesn't depend on it; the legacy builder would run every stage in order. Note that --target takes a stage name, so the stage must be named with AS. COPY --from can also refer to a stage by numeric position, but that becomes fragile the moment anyone reorders or inserts a stage, silently changing what the index points at.

examples.title: Naive Single-Stage vs Multi-Stage for a Compiled Go Service
examples.code:
# Single-stage: ships the entire Go toolchain in production (~800MB+)
FROM golang:1.22
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server .
ENTRYPOINT ["/out/server"]

# Multi-stage: ships only the compiled binary (~15-20MB)
FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server .

FROM alpine:3.19
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
COPY --from=builder /out/server /usr/local/bin/server
ENTRYPOINT ["server"]
examples.explanation: Both images run the same compiled binary and behave identically at runtime; the difference is what else comes along. The single-stage version's final image is the golang:1.22 image, compiler, standard library source, build cache, and all, plus one more layer containing the compiled binary. None of that toolchain is removed just because the build is done. The multi-stage version's final stage starts fresh from alpine (a few MB), adds CA certificates (needed for outbound HTTPS calls, a runtime concern), and copies in only the compiled binary from the builder stage. The Go compiler, module cache, and source tree are never referenced by a COPY --from in the final stage, so they never appear in it.

examples.title: Three Stages: Dependencies, Build, and a Slim Runtime
examples.code:
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM deps AS build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
examples.explanation: The build stage is declared FROM deps, so it starts from deps's completed state, including node_modules, rather than a bare Node image. That's a legitimate way to chain stages when a later stage needs everything an earlier one produced, as opposed to cherry-picking with COPY --from. The runtime stage starts fresh FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim again and inherits nothing from deps or build, including the TypeScript compiler, dev tooling, or raw source files. It installs production dependencies only (npm ci --omit=dev; copying node_modules from deps would drag in the devDependencies too) and pulls forward the compiled dist output from build. The finished runtime image contains no TypeScript compiler, no bundler, and no .ts source files, though building the app required all of them.

examples.title: Running Only the Test Stage in CI with --target
examples.code:
$ docker build --target test -t myapp:ci-test .
# RUN npm test executes during this build, in the same environment the real build uses;
# a failing test fails the build, and the production stage is never built

$ docker build -t myapp:latest .
# with no --target, builds the last stage (production) and the stages it depends on
examples.explanation: --target test tells Docker to build only up through the stage named test and stop there. That suits CI jobs whose only purpose is to run the test suite against a build environment matching production's dependency versions, without building, storing, or tagging the production image on every test run. Omitting --target builds the last stage in the file (and what it depends on) and tags that result, which is why stage order matters: whichever stage is written last becomes 'the image' for a plain docker build.

misconceptions.description: Each new FROM in a multi-stage Dockerfile builds on top of the previous stage, the same way each RUN instruction builds on top of the previous layer within one stage.
misconceptions.clarification: A FROM line starts an entirely new, independent build stage from whatever base image it names -- it does not carry forward any files, installed packages, or layers from an earlier stage. A later stage gets anything from an earlier one only through an explicit COPY --from=<stage> naming the files to bring across (or by starting FROM that stage); anything else is left behind and never appears in the final image.

misconceptions.description: Multi-stage builds are mainly a disk-space optimization -- a 900MB image and a 20MB image behave identically otherwise, so it's a nice-to-have, not something worth prioritizing.
misconceptions.clarification: Disk space is the most visible benefit, not the only one. A smaller image also pulls and pushes faster, which affects deploy latency and any platform that scales by starting fresh containers. It also contains far fewer installed packages (no compiler, no build-time dependency tree, no package manager caches) for a vulnerability scanner to flag. CVEs in tools production never executes still show up on security reports and have to be triaged, simply because the tool exists inside the shipped image.

exercises.prompt: This multi-stage Dockerfile fails to build with an error like 'pull access denied for builder, repository does not exist or may require authorization'. Find the bug.
exercises.code:
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server .

FROM alpine:3.19
COPY --from=builder /out/server /usr/local/bin/server
ENTRYPOINT ["server"]
hints: Compare the name given to the first stage's AS clause against the name referenced in the second stage's COPY --from=.
Stage names have to match exactly, character for character -- Docker doesn't try to guess which stage you probably meant.
Fix it by making both references consistent, in either direction.
exercises.solutionCode:
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server .

FROM alpine:3.19
COPY --from=build /out/server /usr/local/bin/server
ENTRYPOINT ["server"]
exercises.solutionExplanation: The first stage is named build (AS build), but the final stage's COPY --from=builder references builder, a name never declared in the file. Docker doesn't fuzzy-match stage names. When --from doesn't match a stage, Docker treats it as an image name and tries to pull an image called builder, which fails with the pull error above. The fix is making the two names agree: either change the reference to --from=build, or rename the stage to AS builder.

exercises.prompt: Given this Dockerfile, list which of the following exist inside the FINAL image once the build completes: (a) the gcc compiler, (b) the compiled server binary, (c) the main.c source file, (d) apk's package cache from installing ca-certificates.
exercises.code:
FROM gcc:13 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY main.c .
RUN mkdir /out && gcc -static -o /out/server main.c

FROM alpine:3.19
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
COPY --from=builder /out/server /usr/local/bin/server
ENTRYPOINT ["server"]
hints: The final stage starts fresh FROM alpine -- go through each of the four items and ask whether it was ever explicitly copied into THIS stage, or installed directly inside it.
gcc and main.c only exist in the builder stage's own filesystem, which the final image never inherits from automatically.
The apk package cache question is about what --no-cache specifically does at install time inside the final stage itself, not about anything from the builder stage.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Only (b), the compiled server binary, exists in the final image -- it's the one artifact explicitly brought over with COPY --from=builder. (a) gcc and (c) main.c exist only in the builder stage, which is discarded once the build finishes and never contributes anything else to the final image. (d) the apk package cache does NOT exist either, because apk add --no-cache skips writing a local package cache to disk in the first place.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The final stage starts fresh FROM alpine:3.19 and gets two things added: ca-certificates installed via RUN apk add, which lives within this stage, and the compiled server binary pulled forward with COPY --from=builder. gcc and main.c belong to the builder stage's filesystem; nothing in the final stage references them, so they're never in the final image, though gcc was needed to produce the binary that is. The apk package cache is a different kind of gotcha: --no-cache tells apk not to persist its package index or cache during this install, so no cache directory is left behind in this stage, independent of any multi-stage reasoning. (The binary is built with -static because a dynamically linked glibc binary from the gcc image wouldn't run on musl-based alpine.)

assessments.prompt: A Dockerfile has FROM golang:1.22 AS builder followed later by FROM alpine:3.19. Immediately after that second FROM line executes, what does the alpine stage's filesystem contain?
options: An error, because you cannot switch base images partway through a single Dockerfile.
Only the compiled binary from the builder stage; everything else from both images is dropped automatically.
Only whatever alpine:3.19's own image normally provides.
Everything from the builder stage, including the Go toolchain, source files, and compiled binary, plus everything alpine:3.19 normally provides.
assessments.explanation: Each FROM starts a new stage from the named base image's filesystem, with no automatic carryover from any earlier stage; getting anything from builder into this stage requires an explicit COPY --from=builder naming what to bring across. The “Everything from the builder stage, including…” option is wrong because it assumes automatic inheritance, which multi-stage builds specifically do not do. The “Only the compiled binary from the builder…” option is wrong because it assumes Docker automatically figures out 'the one artifact you probably want,' which it never does -- COPY --from is always explicit about paths. The “An error, because you cannot switch base…” option is wrong: multiple FROM lines with different base images are how multi-stage builds work, and the syntax is valid.

assessments.prompt: A Dockerfile defines stages named deps, test, build, and production, in that order. Running `docker build .` with no --target flag builds which stage(s), and what gets tagged as the resulting image?
options: Only the deps stage, since it appears first in the file.
It builds through the last stage written in the file (production here), and production's own result becomes the tagged image.
All four stages, and Docker prompts interactively for which one to tag.
Only whichever stage happens to be named "production", regardless of where it's positioned in the file.
assessments.explanation: With no --target, Docker builds the last stage written in the file and tags its result, which is why stage order matters for a plain build. (With BuildKit it builds only the stages that last stage depends on, so test is skipped here; the legacy builder runs every stage in order. Either way production's result is what gets tagged.) The “Only the deps stage, since it appears…” option is wrong -- deps being first doesn't make it the default target; the LAST stage is. The “All four stages, and Docker prompts interactively…” option is wrong -- Docker never prompts interactively during a build; it's fully deterministic from the Dockerfile and flags given. The “Only whichever stage happens to be named…” option is wrong -- it isn't the name "production" that matters, it's the stage's position as the last one in the file; a differently-named last stage would be tagged instead under identical rules.

assessments.prompt: A Dockerfile has `FROM node:20-slim AS deps`, then `FROM deps AS build`, then later `FROM node:20-slim AS runtime`. What does the runtime stage inherit automatically from deps or build?
options: Nothing at all -- runtime starts completely fresh from node:20-slim's own filesystem.
Everything from deps, because runtime happens to reuse the identical base image tag deps used.
Only node_modules, since that's the most commonly needed artifact in a Node.js project.
Everything from build, since build is the most recently completed stage before runtime begins.
assessments.explanation: Every FROM, including this one, starts an entirely new, independent stage from that exact base image's own filesystem -- reusing the same base image tag (node:20-slim) as deps does NOT create any inherited relationship between the two stages; runtime and deps just start from the same image. Anything runtime actually needs from deps or build must be brought across with an explicit COPY --from. The “Everything from build, since build…” option is wrong -- build being the most recent stage chronologically has no bearing on inheritance; only an explicit FROM <stage-name> or COPY --from=<stage-name> creates a real relationship. The “Only node_modules, since that's the most commonly…” option is wrong -- nothing is copied automatically regardless of how commonly needed it is. The “Everything from deps, because runtime happens…” option is wrong -- sharing a base image tag is not the same as one stage building on another; deps itself started fresh from that same tag too, with no special relationship to runtime as a result.

assessments.prompt: A teammate asks why bother with multiple FROM stages instead of just running apt-get remove (or the alpine equivalent) on the build tools at the end of a single-stage Dockerfile, right after compiling. Explain why that approach doesn't actually work the way they'd expect, and why multi-stage builds are the better solution.
assessments.modelAnswer: Removing packages in a later RUN instruction doesn't shrink the image the way it looks like it should, because of how layers work: each instruction produces its own immutable, stacked layer, and an earlier layer that contains the build tools' files is never edited or shrunk afterward. A later apt-get remove layer only adds whiteout markers that hide those files from the container's view, while the bytes stay in the earlier layer, counting toward the image's size and retrievable by anyone who inspects the individual layers or scans layer contents. So an 'install, compile, then remove the compiler' single-stage Dockerfile can end up with an image just as large as one that left the compiler installed, and a scanner that reads layer contents will still flag CVEs in a compiler that's 'not there' from the container's point of view. A multi-stage final stage sidesteps this: it starts from a clean base image that never had the build tools' layers in its history and receives only the artifacts an explicit COPY --from=builder brings across, so no layer in the final image contains the toolchain. That result is smaller and cleaner than hiding files after the fact within a single stage.

concepts.title: Volumes, Persistence, and Container Networking Basics
concepts.description: A container's writable layer disappears the moment the container is removed, so data meant to outlive a single container -- a database's files, uploaded assets -- needs to live in a volume or bind mount instead; getting containers to talk to each other and to the outside world depends on the same network-namespace model, which behaves differently than most people expect the first time they hit it.
learningObjectives: Explain when a container's writable-layer data is lost, on docker rm, versus preserved, on docker stop/start, and why that distinction matters for reasoning about persistence.
Distinguish a named volume from a bind mount and choose correctly between them for a given scenario.
Explain what docker run -p host:container configures, and why a service running inside a container can still be completely unreachable from the host without it.
Explain why containers on a shared user-defined bridge network can resolve each other by name via DNS, while containers on the default bridge, or on different networks, cannot.
Debug a connection-refused or name-not-found scenario caused by a missing port publish or missing shared network.

sections.heading: The Writable Layer Is Ephemeral, But Not As Fragile As People Assume
sections.body:
The common shorthand 'containers are ephemeral, so don't store anything in them' overstates the danger in one way. A container's writable layer survives docker stop: stopping a container just halts its process; the container object and its writable layer still exist on disk, and docker start on that container resumes with the data intact. It's docker rm that discards the writable layer for good, along with anything that was only written there.

That distinction matters because a lot of real deployment workflows don't just stop and restart the same container -- they remove it and create a brand-new one: any docker run for a fresh deploy, any orchestrator rescheduling a workload onto a different node, any docker compose up after pulling a new image. In each case the old container's writable layer is gone, along with anything only there. A database's data files, uploaded user files, anything that must outlive one container instance has to live elsewhere: a volume or a bind mount.

sections.heading: Named Volumes vs Bind Mounts
sections.body:
Both mechanisms attach storage that lives outside any single container's own writable layer, but they differ in where that storage actually lives and who manages it. A named volume, created with docker volume create mydata, or implicitly via -v mydata:/path if it doesn't already exist, is storage that Docker itself manages -- you refer to it by name, Docker decides where it physically lives on the host's disk, and its lifecycle is fully independent of any particular container: removing the container that was using it does not remove the volume, you'd need docker volume rm or docker compose down -v to take that extra step (docker rm -v removes only anonymous volumes, not named ones). That makes named volumes the right default for something like a database's data directory: you don't care about the exact host path, you care that the data survives container recreation and isn't tied to a specific directory layout on one host.

A bind mount, -v /host/specific/path:/container/path, instead maps one exact, pre-existing host directory directly into the container. This is the right tool when you want the container to see a specific piece of the host filesystem, most commonly a local project's source directory mounted into a development container so that edits in your editor are instantly visible inside it, without rebuilding an image or re-copying files. The trade-off is portability: a bind mount ties your setup to that host's directory layout and permissions, a poor fit for anything meant to run unmodified on a teammate's laptop, in CI, and in production, where a named volume's host-independence fits better.

sections.heading: Container Networking: Each Container Gets Its Own Network Namespace
sections.body:
As the first concept in this subject covered, every container gets its own network namespace by default: its own loopback interface, network interfaces, routing table, and view of which ports are in use. A service listening on port 5432 inside a container listens within that container's private network namespace, with no relationship to port 5432 on the host or in any other container. That's why 'the container shows Up in docker ps and the process inside is listening' doesn't mean you can reach it from your browser at localhost: localhost on the host refers to the host's network namespace, a separate network stack from the container's.

docker run -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT is what actually bridges the two: it configures a NAT (network address translation) port-forwarding rule that takes traffic arriving at the host on HOST_PORT and forwards it into the container's network namespace, to CONTAINER_PORT. Once that's set up, curl localhost:HOST_PORT on the host reaches the service, but the service has no idea any remapping is happening; to it, it's an ordinary process listening on CONTAINER_PORT. Forget -p, and the service is unreachable from the host, however correctly it runs inside the container.

sections.heading: EXPOSE Is Documentation, Not a Publish Instruction
sections.body: A very common point of confusion: the Dockerfile's EXPOSE instruction does not publish anything to the host, and never has. EXPOSE 8080 records metadata on the image saying 'the application inside expects to listen on port 8080'. That's useful as documentation, and some tooling uses it, such as docker run -P (capital P), which publishes every EXPOSEd port to a random host port, but it creates no reachability on its own. A Dockerfile with EXPOSE 8080 and a docker run with no -p produces a running container with a process listening on 8080 inside its own network namespace, unreachable from the host despite the EXPOSE line. Declaring the port in the image and publishing it at run time are separate, and skipping the second is one of the most common beginner mistakes in this subject.

sections.heading: User-Defined Networks and DNS-Based Service Discovery
sections.body:
Two containers reaching each other, rather than a container reaching or being reached from the host, is a separate question. By default, docker run with no --network flag attaches a container to Docker's default bridge network, which, for historical reasons, does not provide automatic DNS resolution between containers on it; reaching another container by name on the default bridge doesn't work, or requires the long-deprecated --link flag.

A user-defined bridge network, docker network create appnet, then docker run --network appnet --name db ... and docker run --network appnet --name api ..., behaves better: every container attached to that same user-defined network gets automatic DNS resolution of every other container's name on that network. From inside the api container, a plain hostname lookup for db resolves directly to db's IP address on that specific network -- no manual IP address bookkeeping, no editing /etc/hosts, no --link. This is the mechanism docker compose relies on: a compose file's services are automatically placed on a shared, project-specific user-defined network, which is why application code in a typical compose setup can connect to a hostname like db or redis with no networking setup visible in the compose file. Two containers started with plain docker run and no shared --network are, by contrast, on the default bridge (no name resolution) or on separate networks, and can't resolve each other by name until you put them on the same user-defined network.

examples.title: Data Survives docker stop/start, But Not docker rm Without a Volume
examples.code:
$ docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpassword -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
# (wait a few seconds for Postgres to finish initializing)
$ docker exec db psql -U postgres -c "CREATE TABLE t(x int); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1);"

$ docker stop db && docker start db
$ docker exec db psql -U postgres -c "SELECT * FROM t;"
# x
# ---
# 1        <- still there, stop/start preserved both the writable layer AND the volume

$ docker rm -f db
$ docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpassword -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
$ docker exec db psql -U postgres -c "SELECT * FROM t;"
# x
# ---
# 1        <- STILL there, because it lives in the named volume pgdata, not in db's writable layer,
#             and pgdata's lifecycle is independent of the container that used it
examples.explanation: The table survives docker stop/start whether or not a volume is involved, since stopping a container never destroys its writable layer. The more important part is what happens after docker rm -f db, which discards that container and its writable layer: a fresh container from the same image with no shared volume would start with an empty Postgres data directory and no table. Because the data directory was mounted from the named volume pgdata rather than living in the container's writable layer, it survived the removal, and the new container, a different container object sharing nothing else with the old one, picks the data back up by mounting the same volume by name.

examples.title: What -p Wires Up, and What Forgetting It Looks Like
examples.code:
$ docker run -d --name web1 -p 8080:80 nginx
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080
200

$ docker run -d --name web2 nginx   # no -p at all
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:80
curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 80: Connection refused
$ docker ps --filter name=web2
# STATUS shows "Up" -- nginx really is running and listening on port 80 INSIDE its own network namespace
examples.explanation: web1's -p 8080:80 sets up a NAT rule forwarding the host's port 8080 into web1's network namespace on port 80, which is why curl localhost:8080 succeeds: the host and the container are separate network namespaces, and that flag bridges them. web2 has no such rule: nginx is running and listening on port 80, correctly, but only within its own private network namespace, which the host's localhost has no path into. docker ps reporting web2 as Up reflects that the process is alive; it says nothing about whether any port has been published to the host, which is separate, opt-in configuration.

examples.title: Two Containers Reaching Each Other by Name on a Shared Network
examples.code:
$ docker network create appnet
$ docker run -d --network appnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpassword --name db postgres:16
$ docker run -d --network appnet --name api myapi:1.0
$ docker exec api getent hosts db
172.18.0.2      db
# "db" resolves via Docker's embedded DNS on appnet

$ docker run -d -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpassword --name db2 postgres:16   # no --network: default bridge
$ docker run -d --name api2 myapi:1.0                                     # same: default bridge
$ docker exec api2 getent hosts db2
# (no output, exit status 2: "db2" doesn't resolve)
examples.explanation: db and api share the user-defined network appnet, which gives every container on it automatic DNS resolution of every other container's name: api looking up db gets db's IP address on that network, with no configuration beyond --network appnet on both. db2 and api2 were started with no --network flag, which lands them on Docker's default bridge network, which for legacy reasons doesn't provide that name resolution. The fix is never a DNS change inside the application; it's placing the containers that need to find each other on the same user-defined network, which is what docker compose does automatically for every service in a compose file.

misconceptions.description: As long as docker ps shows a container as 'Up' and I know the service inside is listening on some port, I should be able to reach it from my host's browser or curl.
misconceptions.clarification: Each container gets its own network namespace, entirely separate from the host's -- a service listening inside a container is only reachable from the host if that specific port was explicitly published with -p HOST:CONTAINER, or -P to auto-publish every EXPOSEd port. docker ps reporting 'Up' only reflects that the container's main process is alive; it says nothing about whether any port-forwarding rule into the host's network namespace has been configured. EXPOSE in the Dockerfile doesn't publish anything either -- it's documentation metadata on the image, not a runtime networking action.

misconceptions.description: A Docker volume is really just a folder that happens to live inside the container, so it's just as ephemeral as anything else written inside a container -- it disappears whenever the container is removed.
misconceptions.clarification: A named volume, or a bind mount, lives OUTSIDE the container's own writable layer and has its own independent lifecycle, which is the point of using one. Removing the container that used a named volume does not delete the volume: the data persists and can be reattached to a new, unrelated container by mounting the same volume name. A named volume is deleted only by an explicit, separate action, docker volume rm or docker compose down -v, never as a side effect of removing whichever container used it last (docker rm -v removes only anonymous volumes).
misconceptions.fact: A named volume, or a bind mount, deliberately lives OUTSIDE the container's own writable layer and has its own independent lifecycle, which is the entire point of using one.

exercises.prompt: A developer runs a web app in a container and says: 'docker ps shows it's Up, but I can't load it in my browser at localhost:3000 no matter what I try.' Find the bug in how they started the container and fix it.
exercises.code:
$ docker build -t myapp .
$ docker run -d --name myapp myapp
$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE    STATUS         PORTS
a1b2c3d4e5f6   myapp    Up 2 minutes
$ curl http://localhost:3000
curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 3000: Connection refused
hints: Look at the PORTS column in that docker ps output -- what would you expect to see there if a port had actually been published to the host?
The app being 'Up' and listening on port 3000 inside its own network namespace has no automatic effect on the host's own port 3000 at all.
You can't add -p to an already-running container -- it has to be specified at docker run time, so the container needs to be recreated with it.
exercises.solutionCode:
$ docker rm -f myapp
$ docker run -d --name myapp -p 3000:3000 myapp
$ docker ps
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE    STATUS         PORTS
f6e5d4c3b2a1   myapp    Up 2 seconds   0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp
$ curl http://localhost:3000
# now succeeds
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original docker run -d --name myapp myapp had no -p flag, so no NAT/port-forwarding rule was created between the host's network namespace and the container's. The app is running and listening on port 3000, but only within its own private network namespace, which the host's localhost has no path into. The empty PORTS column in docker ps confirms that nothing was published. Because -p can only be specified when a container is created, not added to an already-running one, the fix requires removing the existing container and recreating it with -p 3000:3000, at which point docker ps shows the expected 0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp mapping and the host-side curl succeeds.

exercises.prompt: Two containers are started with these commands, with no shared --network flag between them. The api container's code tries to connect to a Postgres database at the hostname db. Predict what happens when it tries, and why.
exercises.code:
$ docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpassword postgres:16
$ docker run -d --name api myapi:1.0
$ docker exec api python -c "import socket; print(socket.gethostbyname('db'))"
hints: Neither docker run specified a --network flag -- what network do containers land on by default when you don't specify one?
Does the default bridge network provide automatic DNS-based name resolution between containers on it, the way a user-defined network does?
The fix isn't a code change inside api -- it's a docker network create plus attaching both containers to it via --network.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It fails with a name resolution error, something like socket.gaierror: [Errno -2] Name or service not known, because both containers landed on Docker's default bridge network with no --network flag specified, and the default bridge does not provide automatic DNS resolution of container names -- db simply doesn't resolve to anything from api's point of view.
exercises.solutionExplanation: With no --network specified, both db and api are attached to Docker's default bridge network, which, unlike a user-defined bridge network, does not run the embedded DNS resolution that maps container names to IP addresses. From inside api, the lookup for db has nothing to resolve against, so it fails outright rather than connecting to the wrong thing or timing out slowly. The fix is to create a user-defined network, docker network create appnet, and start both containers with --network appnet, which is exactly the setup a docker-compose.yml provides implicitly for every service it defines -- at which point the identical socket.gethostbyname('db') call would succeed and return db's actual IP address on that network.

assessments.prompt: You run docker run -d nginx with no -p flag, and the Dockerfile that built the image includes EXPOSE 80. What happens when you then run curl http://localhost:80 from the host?
options: It fails with a permission error, because nginx needs root privileges to bind to port 80 on the host.
It succeeds, but only for the first request, because Docker publishes the first connection attempt automatically.
It succeeds, because EXPOSE 80 in the Dockerfile automatically publishes port 80 to the host.
It fails to connect, because no port was actually published to the host -- EXPOSE is documentation on the image.
assessments.explanation: EXPOSE is purely image metadata/documentation and never publishes a port on its own; only -p/--publish at docker run time, or -P to auto-publish every EXPOSEd port, actually creates the host-to-container port-forwarding rule, and none of those were used here. The “It succeeds, because EXPOSE 80…” option directly misstates what EXPOSE does. The “It succeeds, but only for the first…” option describes behavior Docker has no such 'first request' mechanism for -- it's invented. The “It fails with a permission error…” option is wrong for two reasons: it's not a permission issue, and more fundamentally the request never even reaches the container's network namespace to encounter any such issue, because nothing was published.

assessments.prompt: A named volume `pgdata` is mounted into a Postgres container. The container is later removed with `docker rm -f`. What happens to the volume and its data?
options: The volume persists only if the container was stopped gracefully before removal, not if -f (force) was used.
The volume and its data persist independently of the container's removal.
The volume's data is preserved but becomes permanently read-only after the container that created it is removed.
The volume is automatically deleted along with the container, since it was only ever used by that one container.
assessments.explanation: A named volume's lifecycle is fully independent of any specific container -- removing the container that was using it, forcefully or not, does not delete the volume; only an explicit docker volume rm or docker compose down -v removes it (docker rm -v removes only anonymous volumes). The “The volume is automatically deleted along…” option is the misconception this concept warns against: volumes are not scoped to the container's lifecycle the way the writable layer is. The “The volume's data is preserved but becomes…” option is wrong -- nothing about container removal makes a volume read-only; it remains fully writable by whatever mounts it next. The “The volume persists only if the container…” option is wrong -- the -f flag on docker rm affects whether a running container is stopped first, not whether an attached named volume survives; the volume survives either way.

assessments.prompt: Two containers are started with plain `docker run` commands, neither specifying a --network flag. Why can't one resolve the other by container name?
options: Name resolution requires both containers to have been started from the exact same image.
Name resolution between containers requires at least one of them to have a published port via -p.
Container name resolution only works when both containers are running on the same physical host, which isn't guaranteed here.
Both containers land on Docker's default bridge network, which, unlike a user-defined bridge network, does not provide automatic DNS-based name resolution between containers on it.
assessments.explanation: With no --network specified, both containers attach to the default bridge, which -- for legacy reasons -- doesn't run the embedded DNS resolution a user-defined bridge network provides; creating a network with docker network create and attaching both containers to it fixes this immediately. The “Container name resolution only works when both…” option is wrong -- the two containers ARE on the same host here; the issue is the network they're on, not physical placement. The “Name resolution between containers requires at least…” option is wrong -- publishing a port to the host has nothing to do with inter-container DNS resolution, which is purely about the network they share. The “Name resolution requires both containers to have…” option is wrong -- name resolution has no relationship to which image a container was started from.

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between a named volume and a bind mount, and give one concrete, realistic scenario where you'd specifically choose each.
assessments.modelAnswer: Both attach storage that lives outside the container's own writable layer, so the data survives even if the container is removed. The difference is where that storage lives and who manages it. A named volume is storage that Docker itself creates and manages; you refer to it purely by name, for example -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data, Docker decides where it actually sits on the host's disk, and its lifecycle is fully decoupled from any specific container -- removing the container that used it leaves the volume intact, ready to be reattached to a brand-new container later. This makes named volumes the right choice for something like a production database's data directory: you don't want to hardcode a host path, you want the data to persist across container recreation, deploys, crashes, and rescheduling, without replicating a particular directory structure on another host. A bind mount instead maps one specific, already-existing host directory directly into the container, for example -v /Users/me/project/src:/app/src, giving the container direct, live access to that exact piece of the host filesystem. This is the right choice for local development: mounting your project's source directory into a container so that edits in your editor on the host are instantly visible inside the container, without rebuilding an image or copying files on every change. The trade-off is that a bind mount ties the setup to that host's directory layout and permissions, so it's the wrong tool for anything meant to run unmodified across machines: a teammate's laptop, a CI runner, and a production host are unlikely to share the same absolute path, the portability problem a named volume avoids by design.
